name: Mel-Khaonh
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Only Barr & Pawley 2013 SIL Bahnaric sociolinguistic survey named; no phonological description with stress located.

new_statements.quote: Bahnaric languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages, are sesquisyllabic. Sesquisyllabic languages have a minor syllable and a major syllable. The minor syllable comes first and is unstressed while the following major syllable is stressed. Over time, these minor syllables are subject to innovation and sometimes collapse onto the main syllable, while the major syllable is usually retained and can be reliably reconstructed. In some Mon-Khmer varieties the minor syllable may be lost entirely.
new_statements.citation: Lambrecht, Philip & Noel Mann. 2017. Mel and Khaonh Language Survey Report. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2017-004. Dallas: SIL International.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (minor presyllable + major syllable); the word-final major syllable carries the stress and the preceding minor syllable is unstressed (iambic, stress on the final/main syllable). Stated as a property of Bahnaric languages in general, in the survey report whose authors collected and analysed the Mel and Khaonh wordlists under this assumption.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the report notes only that minor syllables vary or are lost across varieties (e.g. Mel kətʊːl ~ kᵊtʊːl 'abdomen', ᵊraw ~ raw 'wash').
new_statements.domain_note: Generic family-level statement (Bahnaric / Mon-Khmer word structure) used as the premise for stripping minor syllables from the Mel, Khaonh, Stieng, Kraol etc. wordlists; not a description derived from Mel-Khaonh data, no stress marks in the transcriptions, citation-form wordlist items only. This is a sociolinguistic survey report, not a phonological description; Glottolog rates the language's documentation as 'wordlist or less'.
new_statements.identity_note: Lambrecht & Mann 2017 treat Mel ([məl]; villages Roluos, Paklae, Changhab, Srae Tahaenh) and Khaonh ([kʰaoɲ]; Chhork, Kasang) as two closely related lects (88% lexical similarity, marginal intelligibility); ISO/Glottolog merge them as Mel-Khaonh [hkn] = melk1242. The stress-relevant sentence is a generic statement about 'Bahnaric languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages' made in the Mel/Khaonh survey report and applied to the Mel and Khaonh wordlists; it is not an observation stated specifically of Mel or Khaonh forms.

sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey (interviews, wordlists, comprehension test). No phonology chapter. Sec. 2.3.2 (p. 12) states generically that Bahnaric languages, like other Mon-Khmer languages, are sesquisyllabic: the minor syllable comes first and is unstressed, the following major syllable is stressed; minor syllables of the Mel/Khaonh/Stieng/Kraol forms are then stripped for lexical comparison. Mel/Khaonh transcriptions in Table 4 (e.g. Mel kətʊːl 'abdomen', məhaːm 'blood', lᵊpiət 'tongue', ᵊraw 'wash'; Khaonh kəndʊl, məhae, ᵐpeæt) show reduced presyllables consistent with this, but no stress marks…
MED = wordlist_or_less (Lambrecht & Mann 2017); no grammar, sketch or phonology known to Glottolog.

sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey; sec. 4.2.2 'The Khaonh and the Mel' gives only lexical-similarity figures (two Mel and two Khaonh wordlists, 80-95%). Appendices F/G say many Mon-Khmer languages are sesquisyllabic and presyllables were ignored in counting; nothing on stress, nothing Mel/Khaonh-specific.
No phonology; cites only Barr & Pawley 2013 and Ethnologue 21.
